On the motion of Right Hon. R. L. Borden for Committee of Supply:

I
desire to draw attention to the Kitsilano Indian Reserve, which was the subject of discussion on the 24th of April, and upon which further light was thrown by a return brought down dated the 23rd of May. I will read from this return the report of the inspector of Indian agencies which will place the case before the House briefly and clearly, and with more effect than I could. The report is dated, Victoria, April 26, 1913, addressed to the secretary of the Department of Indian Affairs, and Teads:
With further reference to my letter of the Uth instant dealing with the reported surrender of the False Creek Reserve at Van-



couver by certain Indians of the Squamrsh tribe to the provincial government, I beg to state that I have just returned from Vancouver, and wish to confirm the statement contained in the press despatch enclosed with my letter of the 11th instant, in so far as the Indians giving their consent to the sale and receiving the money.
The negotiations with the Indians were Car-Tied on by H. O. Alexander, Esq., stipendiary magistrate of Vancouver, on behalf of the Government of British Columbia. The amount paid to the Indians was $219,750. Nineteen heads of families received $11,250 each and one received' only $5,000, making twenty families in all. The Indians were also paid $1,000 for the removal of the dead bodies from the graveyard. Upon the Indians signing the agreement and receiving the;r money their effects were placed on a scow and towed up the Squamish river to one of the reserves, to which place most of the Indians also went. The expenses in this connection were borne by the British Government.
Mr. Alexander has informed me that he worked on a list which he made up himself, but it does not correspond with the Indian agent's census of this band, for it appears that money was paid to Indians who were not members of the band, while there were members who did not receive compensation. I visited the reserve and found that all the Indians had left.	Their houses
had	been pulled	down	and	burned;
The last house on the water front portion of the reserve was being torn down while I was there on Tuesday, the 22nd, And the workmen informed me that they were (working under the instructions of the provincial government, who also have a policeman on the reserve.
Thi9 is one of the Indian reserves set aside prior to Confederation, and consisted at that time of 37.45 acres: in 1876 (according to the Journal of the Indian Reserve Commission), the Joint Reserve Commission increased the size of the reserve to 80 acres. Since that time 10.52 acres have been sold to the Canadian Pacific railway and the Vancouver and boon Island railway for railroad purposes. The Harrison Mills Timber and Trading Company also have a lease of 11.16 acres of the reserve.
The amount paid to the Indians in consideration of their giving up this reserve ($219,750) appears to he extremely small, so far as land values in that portion of the city of Vancouver are concerned; hut at present, without going into the matter very fully, it is impossible to state definitely as to the true value of the reserve. However, it would not be very wide of the mark to say that it is worth at least ten times the amount paid to the Indians.
It appears from the return that not only did the British Columbia Government remove the Indians from the reserve, burn or pull down their buildings, and establish police authority upon the reserve, but they publicly advertised the jurisdiction of the British Columbia Government over the reserve by notice in tlhe British Columbia Gazette, as follows:
Mr. OLIVER
Department of Lands,
Notice of Reserve.
Notice is hereby given that the certain portion of land officially known as Burrard Inlet Reserve No. 6, and commonly called Kitsilano or False Creek reserve, situated on the south side of the entrance to False Creek and arm or Burrard Inlet, and containing 80 acres, more or less, is reserved from any entry or alienation under the Mineral Act, the PlacerMining Act, the Coal and Petroleum Act, or the Land Act.
Robert A. Renwick, Deputy Commissioner of Lands, Department of Lands,
Victoria, B.C., April 11, 1913.
It (will be observed that the Indians left the reserve on April 9, and, on April 11, the British Columbia Government gazetted its assertion of authority, over the property rights within the reserve. I brought this transaction to the attention of the House and the answer to my question is dated Monday, April 21, 1913. My question was as follows;
Is the Government aware of steps being taken, as alleged, to acquire from the Indians of tihe Kitsilano reserve, Vancouver,
B.C., their rights to the land of the reserve by the provincial government of British Columbia, or by other parties or interests?
The answer to that question was; 'No.'

It is evident, therefore, that the Government had knowledge of this transaction being in progress and that they took no measure to prevent its being carried forward. So far as we are aware, they have taken no measures to readjust the conditions since the arrangement between the British Columbia Government and the Indians was made; and I submit that the condition is such as to call for a very full explanation from the Government of its position and intentions in the matter.
This document also discloses that a part of this reserve, some thirty-seven acres, was set apart by Governor Sir James Douglas, acting as the direct representative of the British Crown while administering the affairs of what is now British Columbia as a Crown colony. Therefore, there can be no question as to the proprietary rights on the part of this band of Indians to that much of their reserve in any case. In the remarks I had the honour to make some time ago in this connection, I pointed out that the responsibility and control of Indian Affairs was a trust transferred from the Imperial authorities to this Dominion Government, and that there was no means whereby they could properly divest themselves 'of that responsibility. There is some question raised by the British Columbia Government in regard to proprietary rights of the Indians in the class of reserve more recently set apart, but there can be no valid contention made against the absolute right of the Indians to the thirty-seven acres of this reserve received by direct title from the Imperial Government, nor can there be any question of the responsibility of this Government to absolutely protect the Indians in the full enjoyment of their rights in that portion of the reserve, and equally in their right to secure full value for the land should the transfer of that land be made.
This case is the more remarkable because there is an arrangement between the Government of British Columbia and this Mr. OLIVER.
Government for the settlement of the questions at issue between these Governments in regard to Indian reserves. The basis of agreement has been arrived at and a commission has been appointed. Under that arrangement and by the work of that commission, this particular reserve would undoubtedly have been dealt with, and the Government of British Columbia would have been maintained in whatever right it had according to the arrangement arrived at.
Apparently the Government of British Columbia, whether with or without the consent and knowledge of this Government, have seen fit to enter upon this property and assert the right of that Government, irrespective of this agreement. That is to say, they have made an agreement with the Dominion Government, and before that agreement becomes effective they take measures, aside from the agreement, to establish a property right which, in my estimation, they have not at all and would not have under the terms of this agreement.
The Dominion Government, charged with the responsibility of protecting the rights of the Indians, both as to their property and as to their persons, having made an agreement with the Government of British Columbia for the proper adjustment of all these rights according to their judgment, permit the Government of British Columbia to go outside of that agreement, to deal with those Indians in a manner absolutely contrary to the law, to remove them from the reserve, to destroy their property upon the reserve, to assert the authority of the provincial Government in regard to that reserve, and that on a payment of money that is stated even by the officer of this Government to be less than one-tenth of the actual value of the land. I submit that the Government are deserving of censure and of serious censure, unless they can give some better explanation of the case than they gave on the former occasion.
Coming now to the discussion of the arrangement between the Government of the province and the Government of the Dominion ; the provincial Government claims that the Indians do not own this land, that it belongs to the provincial Government, that the Indians have only a right of occupation, and that when the Indians leave the land, the title of the British Columbia Government to that land at once accrues. As I have already said, it was not possible for the Dominion Gov-* ernment to agree to that proposition, and the late Government had arrived _ at an agreement with the British Columbia Government to submit the question, as a legal case, to the judgment of the Privy Council. Later on the British Columbia Government refused to go on with that agreement. Still later this Government took the matter up

and arrived at an amicable arrangement with the British Columbia Government; and as soon as the agreement was arrived at- the British Columbia Government proceeds forthwith to set it aside; they take action independently; and this Government, so far as our returns show, has done absolutely nothing to protect the rights of the Indians in the matter.
In regard to the merits of the arrangement made between the Dominion and the province for the disposition of the rights of the Indians, I can only say that in my humble judgment it is an agreement which is intended to make peace between the province and the Dominion at the expense of the Indians. Under this arrangement the right of the province is admitted wherever the Indians have vacated their reserve or a* portion of their reserve. That is to say, the province claims that wherever the Indians have vacated their reserve the land belongs to the province and not to the remainder of the Indians, and this Government by its arrangement concedes that subject to sale and equal division of the proceeds between the province and the Dominion. The British Columbia Government has secured the vacation of this reserve by payment to the Indians of a quarter of a million -dollars, and claim the absolute ownership of the property. I assume it is in that view that the British Columbia Government have acted.
As to the fairness or reasonableness of such an agreement being entered into whereby the two Governments undertake to dispose of the rights of the Indians without considering what those rights are, without having those rights decided by that authority which is and ought to be the final court of appeal in regard to all such cases, it is a departure from precedent as to the proper discharge of the responsibilities of the Government of Canada in regard to the Indian tribes. It is disregarding the trust that has been placed on this Government by the Imperial authorities in regard to the rights of the Indians, and is net such an arrangement as can be considered to be fair and reasonable or in consonance with the dignitv of the Government of Canada or the responsibilities that properly rest on that Government.
The question of the price cf this land is not a serious matter. The serious matter is that this Government has seen fit-and I am bound to say, on the evidence of this return, that they have seen fit with knowledge-to forego their responsibility of protecting the rights of those Indians in Tegard to that land. They have done it without reason, because there is legislation on the Statute Book which can be brought into play that would effectually protect both the rights of the Indians and the rights of the
people of Vancouver. They have not seen fit to bring that legislation into action. They have seen fit to allow an unwarranted assertion of authority by the British Columbia Government which is neither more nor less than piracy, in taking these Indians ofl their land, burning their houses, in establishing control and asserting ownership of this land, without, so far as this return shows, ever referring the matter to this Government, although it is also shown that this Government had knowledge of the transaction. These are serious matters. When it is established, as it is established, that the Indians have been paid a quarter of a million dollars for land that is worth ten times as much, surely that concrete fact will appeal very strongly to the people of Canada .as establishing the failure of the Government to exercise their proper responsibilty in protecting the rights of those Indians. They have made an agreement with the British Columbia Government. It is an unfair agreement; but if that agreement was being carried out there might be some justification. What has been done has been done in defiance ot that agreement, without regard to it, that is, without regard to its letter; and, so .far as we are aware, this Government has taken no means, directly or indirectly, either to protect the riglits of the Indians in the first place or to restore those rights now that they have so far been taken away from them. They have taken no means to bring into play the legislation af this Parliament, that was provided particularly and especially for meeting just such cases in .a fair and equitable manner.
Right Hon. R. X. BORDEN (Prime Min-i=ter) [DOT] My hon. friend has traversed a good deal of the ground which he went over at very considerable length about a month ago. I am not aware that he has brought to the attention of the House any material circumstances that were not made known then. As he has stated, there is a commission which is investigating the whole question of Indian affairs in the province of British Columbia, and, having been Minister of the Interior for a number of years, he knows, or ought to know, that the rights of the Indians in respect to their lands in the province of British Columbia, or anywhere else, can only be interfered with under the law of this country, and there are two statutes which are available for that purpose. My hon. friend says that there has been an agreement between this Government and the province of British Columbia by which this Government would undertake to do anything that the British Columbia Government might find satisfactory to the Indians.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council

speechtext:
My right hon. friend has not at all submitted to the House the point at issue. It is quite true that the relations of the Indian with the white man are regulated by those statutes; but on the present occasion the point is that neither statute has been followed; both have been ignored. Neither the general statute for the surrender of reserves nor the Indian Act has been followed. It was only two or three years ago that a Bill was introduced in this House to meet a case similar to the present one. That was the case of the Songhees Indians of Victoria. By experience we know that Indian reserves in the vicinity of growing cities are a detriment, not only to the growing cities, but to the Indians themselves, and it is in their own interests that they should be removed from those cities, or their immediate neighbourhood. At the present time the Indians can surrender their rights under the Indian Act; but this requires their consent, and there have been cases in which the Indians have not been willing to give their consent. That was the case of the Songhees Indians at Victoria. The matter had been under discussion between the authorities of Victoria and the Indians, and the Indians always refused to agree to the surrender. At last the Government of British Columbia took the matter up and obtained the consent of the Indians. That? was the occasion upon which I sent the telegram, wthich was quoted some time ago by my hon. friend, and which has been quoted
again to-day, to Sir Richard McBride, stating that the price and conditions, if acceptable to the Indians, would be acceptable to us. The matter had been considered for some years, and the only point was to obtain the consent of the Indians. The conditions that were offered by the Government of British Columbia on behalf of the city of Victoria were acceptable and reasonably fair. We knew that the Government of British Columbia were anxious to have the consent of the Indians, we were willing and anxious to have their consent, and we advised the Government of British Columbia that we would be willing to agree to those conditions. But there is a difference between the Songhees case and this.
In order that the House may understand this question, let me point out that the Indians may surrender their rights; but if they do so, it must be done with the consent and approval of the Superintendent General of Indian Affairs. If the Indians, although they are so advised by him, will not surrender their rights, then the authorities who want the surrender can apply to the Court of Exchequer and obtain judgment of the court as to whether the Indians shall be removed or dispossessed. We thought it would not be fair to dispossess the Indians, even though we thought it was in their own interests, unless we had judicial authority for so doing. We wanted to preserve the sacredness of the trust which has been imposed upon us, as upon all British governments, with reference to the interior races before dispossessing them of their land. But if the Indians are willing to surrender their reserve, as was the case with the False Creek Teserve, you must have the consent of three parties: first, the purchaser-in this case the Government of British Columbia; next, the Indians; and next, the Superintendent General of Indian Affairs. In this case the Superintendent General of Indian Affairs did not participate in the negotiations at all. There was the consent of the Indians' and the consent of the British Columbia Government; but it appears that the Superintendent General of Indian Affairs simply surrendered his rights altogether. The correspondence shows that the Superintendent knew that negotiations weTe going on, but did not interfere at all. My hon. friend (Mr. Crothers) may shake his head, but I would be very glad to have his explanation upon this point.
My hon. friend from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) presented the case to the House fairly and moderately, and his conclusion is that, if the facts are as they have been presented, the Government are censurable. But he says: I do not want to ask for the

censure of the Government to-day; I -want the explanation of the Government. If the facts are as disclosed by my hon. friend from Edmonton, and if this transaction has taken place with the consent of the Superintendent General of Indian Affairs, then he has been imprudent in his conduct; but if he has not given his consent to this transaction, the Government are *certainly highly censurable, because they have been altogether recreant to the duty imposed upon them by the law for the protection of the Indians. As we know, the Indian is the ward of the nation; he is treated as an Indian; he cannot sell a pelt unless he has the consent of the Superintendent General of Indian Affairs, through the agent; and shall it be said on this occasion that the Indians can sell their rights to the land which they occupy without the consent of the Superintendent General of Indian Affairs? That is the charge which was made by my hon. friend, and upon which he desires information.
The question as to the general right of the government of a province with reference to the lands now in possession of the Indians is a very large one, and I shall not enter upon the discussion of it at the present moment. But that is 'not a matter in issue at the present time. The question is whether the sale was authorized by the Superintendent General of Indian Affairs. If not, the whole transaction is null and void, and there is no title conveyed to anybody. Do I understand that these men, without the consent of the Superintendent General of Indian Affairs, paid $200,000 for this property, when there was another party ready to offer $2,000,0o0? Do I understand that, as alleged, the Government allowed these 'Indians to be deprived of their rights?-because the British Columbia Government have no rights to these lands, unless they have the signature of the Superintendent General of Indian Affairs. Do I understand that without having that authority they have dispossessed the Indians, burned their homes over their heads, and forced them to leave and settle elsewhere? That is the point upon which we must have some information so as to ascertain exactly what has been the conduct of the Government in the matter.

speakeroldname: Hon. T. W. CROTHERS (Acting Minister of the Interior):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this matter was before the House about a month ago, and there was an answer given at that time to some observations made by my right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) and also to some made by the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver). In face of the explanations that were then given, my right hon. friend asks the question now as to whether the Government were consulted as Sir WILFRID LAURIER.
to this surrender. Did they agree that these Indians should be paid a quarter of a million for property that is worth $2,000,000? All that was answered a month ago, but I do not mind repeating it now; it will not take very much time. I told my right hon. friend then that we had not been communicated with at all in respect to this matter. I told him then that we had not given our consent and I can only repeat that now. I quite agree with him that the Indians have no right to dispose of their interests without the consent of the Government.

How is it
that their homes were burned over their heads?
Not over their heads. They went to another reserve. I do not know whether their homes were burnt over their heads.	-
That is said in the report.

The Government did
not consent in this matter. The whole question will be taken up by the commission which has been appointed to investigate. They were instructed to investigate this whole matter and report. What is the use of asking these questions again, amdi charging the Government with wrongdoing when we have appointed a commission to inquire into the facts?

Do I understand that the Government are proposing to fold their arms, that they do not know whether the Indians have been dispossessed or not, that they do not recognize that they have any duty towards these Indians?

Those questions will
arise when we know what the facts are.
There are the facts reported by the commissioner.

speakeroldname: Hon. ROBERT ROGERS (Minister of Public Works):
speechtext: I would like to say a word or two in connection with some of the statements that have been made. The right hon. leader of the Opposition would seek to leave the impression that the Government are blameable for not having taken certain action. He undertakes to point out to the House that before this transaction could be carried out there must be consent on the part of the Government of British Columbia, on the part of the Indians and on the part of the Indian Department.
Hear, hear.

The fact is that the Indian Department have not dealt with this matter, if I understand it, in any particular, and my right hon. friend and the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) appar-ently-*seek to present, even in the vague

1084E
manner in which they have done so, to this House and the country, that the Indian Department have been responsible or negligent in the discharge of the sacred trust that is imposed upon them in dealing with the Indians. That is a statement to which I wish' to direct a few observations. We absolutely deny negligence in respect to this Indian reserve or to any other Indian reserve in Canada. The acting Minister of the Interior has made clear that no consent has been given by his department, and that consent will not be given until we have the report of the commission now sitting in British Columbia to investigate the Indian titles in that province.
In the meantime the Indians have been dispossessed.

What, apparently is true, is, that the British Columbia Government have followed the example of the manner in which they were able to deal with the Indian trust under the administration of my right hon. friend. The Prime Minister made it clear that in 1910, when the Song-hees reserve was being similarly dealt with, the position taken by the right hon. the leader of the Opposition, then Prime Minister, was: well, if the Indians are satisfied we are satisfied and we will carry it out under the Indian Act.
I draw attention to the fact that the arrangement in regard to the Songhees reserve was brought down to Parliament for the sanction of Parliament.

It was made in the first place without any sanction of Parliament. According to a telegram from Sir Wilfrid Laurier to the Premier of British Columbia, the arrangement was made in the first place and probably the British Columbia Government have gone on thinking that the same manner of treatment of the Indians would be allowed to-day. But the acting minister has made it clear that this Government is not doing business as did the late Government in connection with the sacred trust of the guardianship of the Indians. We will protect that sacred trust. I protest against the right hon. the leader of the Opposition and the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) making the implied insinuations they do. It ill becomes the hon. member for Edmonton and members on that side of the House to talk of the sacred trust of the Indians and the manner in which the Indians are being dealt with to-day, in view of the manner in which they dealt with that sacred trust when they were in power. How did the late Government deal with that sacred trust in western Canada when the hon. gentleman was Minister of the Interior? He dealt with it by peddling the Indian lands out to the liberal organizers and
his liberal friends in Saskatchewan. The public records show that contrary to the Indian Act, contrary to the practice, the lands that were surrendered by the Indians on the specific terms that these lands should be sold by public auction were sold by private sale and peddled out to liberal organizers and the liberal presidents and their friends in Saskatchewan, in defiance of the terms of surrender made by the Indians themselves. That was the manner in which the Indian sacred trust was dealt with while the liberals were in power. To give you an idea of how the sacred trust was regarded by my hon. friend (Mr. Oliver), let me read this extract from a letter:
Yorkton, Sask., July 29, 1910. Frank Pedley, Esq.,
Deputy Superintendent General of Indian Affairs. Ottawa, Can.
My Dear Mr. Pedley,-
I am enclosing some correspondence re a* portion of the surrendered portion of the Cote Indian reserve.
Some of our friends at Kamsack, together with myself, are very anxious to obtain some of this land for the Dixon families. There are quite a number of them, all good farmers, fairly well to do, possessed of families, and friends of ours, and it seems a shame that outside parties are capable of having this land held up, thus preventing settlement and getting desirable parties to improve and settle on these lands.
That letter is signed by Dr. Cash. Here is another letter which I may read:
Yorkton, July, 27, 1910.
Frank Pedley, Esq.,
Deputy Superintendent General, Indian Affairs, Ottawa, Ont.
My Dear Pedley,-
I herewith enclose to you a letter and draft for $96,000. The enclosed letter will tell you what I want, and I certainly think you should make an effort to let Mr. Dixon have this land, as he will be a benefit to the country. There are quite a number of them, and they therefore would also be a benefit to ns in the future.
I think if Mr. McBrady has only made application and not paid for this land, the enclosed application should be considered. Kindly let me hear from you at your earliest convenience, and ablige.
Yours very truly,
(Sgd.) E. L. Cash.
According to the memorandum of the department, Dr. Cash had something like over one hundred quarter sections of this kind at his disposal to peddle out by private sale to his friends in that portion of the territories, notwithstanding that these gentlemen to-day talk about the sacred trust of the Indians. That was the manner in which the Indian trust was being dealt with by hon. gentlemen opposite and they undertake now to try by implication to reflect discredit upon the management of

the Indian Department under the present Administration. It ill becomes hon. gentlemen opposite to make any reflection upon the manner in which the Indian Department is being carried on by the present Administration. I might follow this up further, but I do not propose to do so today, and I might show from the records of this House that even hon. gentlemen who sit upon that side of the House have been peddling these quarter sections themselves, in order that they might make profit, in defiance of the surrender as made by the Indians stipulating that the lands should be sold by public auction. And yet these gentlemen stand up to-day and talk about the sacredness of the trust of the Indians, and make implied insinuations that something has been wrong in connection with this particular reserve. The Prime Minister and the acting Minister of the Interior have made plain the position the Government occupies in this matter. We have given no consent; we purpose giving no consent until the commission now in British Columbia has properly investigated this matter, and we will see that the sacred rights of the Indians are protected in this particular Indian reserve, as in all other reserves in every part of the Dominion.
The hon. member (Mr. Rogers) made a very special reference to my administration, and I wish to say-

Would the minister say on what principle the improvement of air brake valves is chargeable to capital? I do not wish to be discourteous nor do I wish to limit the minister in his answer, but I would rather he would net tell me that the old Government did the same as this. I know that. I am asking for information, and I would like to know on what ground or principle the previous Government and governments before that Mr. ROGERS. -
and the present Government have charged (these things to capital. It seems to me it would be a great consolation to the people of Canada if they really could know what is the condition of the Intercolonial railway. The minister comes down to the House and says : I have a surplus of $500,000; or he comes down and says there is a deficit of $300,000 or $400,000. During the last three or four years there have been what are called surpluses. But we know that there has been no surplus in fact. If all were charged up that ought to be charged up against income, there would be a deficit, as a matter of fact. The minister may say that other roads keep their books in the same way.	That may be
true. But I would like to know on what principle such expenses a3 these are charged to capital. If he would tell us that, we should have a better chance to judge of what is the real position with regard to the Intercolonial railway. It .will not make any difference to the people; they have to pay it anyhow, whatever it is; and if they could know what the actual position is, it would be so much the better. In many cases it is claimed they are not paying high enough rates on the Intercolonial railway. I think that that is not true. But it seems to me it would be better to understand the basis of these so-called surpluses, and if the minister would give us this information it would help.
I have not here the amount charged to capital.
That does not matter-say four and a half millions.

I will have the
figures later. The same system is adopted on the Intercolonial railway as is adopted on other roads in America-in the United States under the Interstate Commerce law. Nothing is charged to capital on the Intercolonial railway that would not be charged to capital on other roads. As to the bookkeeping, I suppose the surplus is ascertained by deducting the expenses and cost of upkeep from the income. I think that anybody can see the results from the figures of income and expense year by year.
I know that.

What more can I
give?
The minister says that they charge up running expenses and upkeep. If they did that, it seems to me that we should have different returns from what we have.

No, the hon. gentleman ha3 misunderstood me. We charge to capital just what others would charge-the

Canadian Pacific railway, for instance. They charge their running expenses just as we do; they are compelled to do so under the law

I admit that. But 1
want the minister to tell me on what principle the Government charges to capital sums that are spent in the running and upkeep of the road.
We do not.
Let us see. Here in the next item you have an estimate for the strengthening of bridges. Is not that keeping up the road?
No.

What is it for, then?
If I have a farm and have to build a road through one portion of it, that is to keep up my farm is it not? And if I have a plough and mowing machine that wear out and have to buy new ones, that is keeping up the farm, is it not?

But if you have a
bridge that is sufficient for the small engines and trains of twenty years ago and you want to strengthen it and improve it to suit modern traffic, that means that your road is that much better. With the expenditure the hon. gentleman speaks of, his farm would be worth more on capital account, would it not?

As the hon. gentleman asks me the question, I can only say that his answer is not a proper one, according to my view of the case. While it is true my farm is worth more, yet I make the expenditure because it is necessary to carry on my farm. If I keep charging up to capital all that I put into the farm, I shall soon find myself bankrupt, although every year my bookkeeping may have shown a surplus. I do not want the minister to think I am finding fault with him. He is doing what other Governments have done. But I want to know the principle upon which it is done. I would like to have it so arranged that the showing of a surplus on the Intercolonial railway would mean that the people of Canada are getting back some return on the money they invested in the road. But we know that to-day that is not the fact. I suppose that in the last ten years the road has, every year been behind from a million to seven or eight million dollars, if you charge to upkeep what you ought to charge. But the supporters and newspapers of the Minister ol Railways come out with the bold statement- just as did the supporters and newspapers of his predecessors-that owing to the splendid management there is a surplus on the road. But on what principle is this kind of bookkeeping carried on?
Would it not be a proper charge against capital, if you had a bridge that cost $100,000, and you were going to strengthen and improve it to 'carry heavier trains?

I do not think so. If
the conditions of traffic change so that the strengthening of that bridge becomes necessary, it seems to me that the road ought to be in a position to make that change without a charge against capital. But under our present system that is charged up to capital, and a surplus is shown where there is really a deficit.
Any farmer, merchant or businessman could show surpluses in the same way. But if any such man attempts to fool himself, he is going to be undeceived before very long.
What would the hon. gentleman allow to be charged to capital? Would he allow the original cost of the road?

Yes. And if the minister were to build a mile or two of railway extra, I would charge that to capital. But I think it requires a great stretch of imagination to think that such work as the strengthening of a bridge or improvement of cars should be charged to capital.
Bridges, to strengthen, $190,000.
Is this for strengthening the bridges on some of the branch lines?

One of the heaviest
expenditures under the item is on the West river bridge at Antigonish, which costs $'65,000. Then, there are the bridges at Keenans and at Nashwaak river on the Canada Eastern, the last $59,000.
That is at Fredericton.

The Canada Eastern
goes down to Fredericton.

An answer was given by a very prominent railway man to the question of what ought to be charged to capital. He said:	'Anything that adds to
value ought to be charged to capital.' If a nail driven into a piece of property increases the value of that property, the cost of the nail can be charged to capital. That is the definition given, I think, in connection with the Interstate Commerce laws. It is rather difficult, however, to carry it out. In the United States the law is framed so as to prevent railway companies from charging things to revenue. The reason for that is that the shareholders of the companies might never get any dividends if everything was charged to revenue. On the Intercolonial we thought we had the matter worked out pretty well along the lines of the Interstate Commerce Commission. The law is

made in the interests of the shareholders as well as in the interests of the directors or the managers. It is necessary under that law that certain things should be charged to capital, and the Interstate Commerce Commission go a long way in order to protect the shareholder and to see that he gets his profits.

The hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell) could get the rates by taking what is charged to capital and computing the interest from that. He rightly says there has never been a proper surlus on the Intercolonial. It has always
een computed on expenditure and receipts. The capital of the Intercolonial, I think, is now about $90,000,000, so that he can easily form his conclusions by adding three per cent, or whatever interest he choses to add to that, and then he gets the surplus or deficit.

The minister ought to
give us a proper statement. He is asking for $7,239,000 for the Intercolonial this year to be charged to capital. I quite appreciate that, under the ordinary acceptance of the the term a portion of that vote could be charged to capital. For instance, he proposes to build the Chatham, $128,000. That is a new line and I think any business man would charge that to capital. The same as the case with dividing the line to Nelson and Derby Junction. While I have some doubt about the wisdom of the move, if it is done, I think it ought to be charged to capital. Among the items, however, I find safety appliances for equipment. Then I find rolling stock, a million dollars.

I wish it were three
million dollars.

The hon. minister will tell us when we come to that point whether that means entirely new stock. Take an illustration. I can understand that, when a road has first been put in operation, it would be fair to charge the rolling stock to capital account, because it is as necessary for the operation of that road as is the roadbed. Let us say the hon. minister buys an engine for $10,000 or $15,000. He runs that engine for ten or fifteen years, and keeps repairing it from time to time. At the end of fifteen years it is like the one-horse shay: it is practically gone. That engine has contributed to the money which the minister says he has received on account of revenue. Without that engine he could never have operated his road. He has made big profits from it. When that engine is worn out, it has answered its purpose in making money for the minister; he buys a new engine and charges that up to capital. That is my point.

When we come to
that item, I shall discuss it.
Mr. GRAHAM.

The same thing with
cars and so on. I judge from the way my hon. friend looks that he is going to explain that. I wonder what becomes of all the repairs and replacing of cars and engines, if they are not charged up to capital account. I hope my hon. friend will give an explanation. I am not asking these questions with any party or fault-finding spirit. I always felt we ought to have a detailed financial statement as to the operation of the Intercolonial. We ought to know exactly what it is costing us to carry on our road. If we are not making a profit, we ought to adjust the business of the road, so as to do so.

I shall be glad to give the explanation desired.

I would like to explain to the House the situation in respect to this vote. It is rather an unusual thing for a member representing a county not to support a resolution granting an expenditure of money in his county, but my reasons for opposing this vote are as follows:	Some
thirty-five years ago there was a move on foot to build a railway between Fredericton and end at or near Derby Junction. It seemed to be a difficult proposition to get a company to undertake this work. A charter was obtained from the local government, and a subsidy was promised by the Dominion Government, as well as by the local government. After the charter had been obtained, it was thought advisable in the interests of the county generally, and of the district to build the road to connect with what was then known as the Chatham branch railway. That branch railway was owned by the late Governor Snowball, who with others, interested himself in the construction of the line between Fredericton and eastwards through Northumberland county. He received the consent of the local government to build the line, according to the routing, as far as Blackville, and then to follow the southwest branch of the Miramiehi and connect at Chatham Junction, thus giving a through line between Chatham and Fredericton. As soon as this became known, friction seemed to arise on the part of the residents of Newcastle on the other side of the river, and through our late respected member of Parliament, the Hon. Peter Mitchell, application was made to the Government to build a branch line on the opposite side of the river, on the north side of the Miramiehi. This was agreed to, but the Dominion Government refused to give a subsidy for the line on the south side of the river between Blackville and Chatham Junction for the reason that they themselves were building a line on the other side of the river. That line for which the subsidy was refused was constructed by the company who had received the charter and the local subsidy, and the line on the opposite side of the river was built by the Dominion Government, and operated, I think, for about fifteen miles between Derby Junction and a point known as lndiantown. The Dominion Government compelled the Canada Eastern to build a connection between Blackville and lndiantown, a distance of about six miles. This, however, was not operated, and the line lay dormant
for some fifteen or twenty years. About the time I became member for the county of Northumberland, the Dominion Government decided to take over the line known as the Canada Eastern railway, built by Mr. Snowball and others, under the circumstances I have just mentioned. In taking over the line between Fredericton and Log-gieville, they also took over the piece of line on the opposite side of the river between Blackville and lndiantown, a distance of about five or six miles, which, as I have said, had laid dormant for a great number of years. On behalf of the people of Newcastle, and especially on behalf of the people of Blackville and Millerton, where the Government branch line was, I applied to the Minister of Railways to put in operation the connecting link of five miles, and the Government did so. So that for the last three years the line has been operated between Newcastle and Blackville, a distance of about twenty-five miles.
Now, the facts are that the people on the south side of the rjver, had, as I have explained, a railway for some thirty-five years, built under a charter granted by the local government. Some seven or eight years ago, the Dominion bought that line, paying the Alexander Gibson Railway Company $750,000 for the property. We have put the connecting link in good condition, and we are now operating a daily train between Blackville and Newcastle direct. The line bought by the Dominion Government is operated regularly, there being an express train each way daily between Loggieville and Fredericton via Chatham Junction. I understand that this vote of $128,000 is for the purpose of conecting Nelson, which is now on the route of the main line, between Fredericton and Loggieville, with Derby Junction. It is alleged that the Government propose taking up the rails on the south side of the river between Nelson and Blackville. For a portion of the distance, 26 miles, the Government granted a subsidy, but for another portion there was no Dominion subsidy granted at all. The road has been operated during the last thirty-five years and the residents of the district feel that they have a vested right. About three miles from Nelson there is a village, the post office at which place is known as Reynolds, and you will find passengers getting on nearly every train at Chatham or Nelson and getting off at Reynold's or at what is known as Ivory's Crossing. Then the railway follows up the south side of the river via Chatham Junction until it arrives at Blackville. En route there are several quite large settlements but the country is not thickly populated at all. Chelmsford is perhaps the principal village between Chelmsford Junction and Blackville on the south side of the river. I am speaking for the people of
I

Chelmsford, because to all intents and purposes, I live at Chelmsford. I do not actually live there, but as far as representing that district is concerned, I live at Chelmsford, and I feel that the people of Chelmsford have good cause for complaint if they are deprived of railway privileges that they have enjoyed for the last thirty or forty years. Looking at it from the economic standpoint, from the amount of money that would be involved, I do not think it is a very important consideration. I have no doubt that when the minister replies to me he will tell me that he is going to give us a better service than that which we at present have on the south side of the river. But that is not an answer to me or to the people on the south side of the river, if you remove the rails which have afforded the facilities for the last thirty-five or forty years. At the present time there are two railway bridges which it would probably cost to rebuild anew of concrete, about $200,000. That, I think, is all the expenditure which would be necessary if you continue following the dines on each side of the river. I am not an engineer, nor do I profess to be, but I have no doubt that $200,000 would he eaten up in providing the necessary terminal facilities at Derby junction. There is $128,000 in the estimates for the purpose of providing for the construction of a line between Nelson and Derby Junction, a distance of about two and a half miles. The Government propose building a line of two and a half miles and doing away with the line of 26 miles, if I understand. Of course, this is surmise on my part, because I have no authority to say, except that I can only read between the lines, what this $128,000 is for.
I would like the committee to consider the situation as if they lived along the south side of the southwest branch of the Mira-michi river, as if they had enjoyed railway privileges for many years and as if they had given their lands as a right of way at a nominal sum. Now they have not even bridge connection across the river, and it is not possible to get across the river for about 15 miles, perhaps 18, between Nelson and what is known as Indiantown. I think the minister ought to weigh the matter well in the interest of all concerned and especially in the interest of the settlement known as Reynolds, between Nelson and Chatham junction and the settlements of Chelmsford and Kirk's between Chatham junction and Blackville. I do not think that money considerations ought to enter into the question at all because the difference in cost will not he very great. I assume that there would be a saving in the cost of upkeep. The minister would tell me probably that he will save the upkeep of twenty-six miles as against the upkeep of three miles. That, Mr. LOGGIE.
I have no doubt, would be some saving, but even considering all the circumstances from an economic standpoint, 1 do not think the minister should undertake to remove the rails of these twenty-six miles and to give us a new line of three miles without giving the people who will be affected thereby some consideration. I know that it has been suggested that bridges would be constructed opposite to most of the populous settlements on the south side of the river and that the people could get rail connection on the other side of the river. That has been alleged, but even so, I find that the residents of that portion of the country are very strongly opposed to the Government removing the rails. They have had public meetings, they have made public representations to the Board of Trade of Chatham, and the Board of Trade has forwarded these representations to the Minister of Railways and Canals, and I have no doubt they have received his favourable consideration. I do not know what his decision is, but it has been suggested that the minister may not go on with this, that possibly the money may be voted and the work not actually performed. But, I think it my duty representing the residents on the south side of the river, to protest in their name against the Government taking away privileges that they have enjoyed for so many years. The Government own a piece of railway on the north side of the river, they bought the railway on the south side of the river and it seems to me that this is a very strong reason why they should continue to operate the line on the south side.
I want to point out what, to some extent, has caused this friction. The minister, and especially the deputy minister, very well knows that the line between Chatham junction and Fredericton is operated westward for the reason that the trains connect with the maritime mail trains. A train leaving Montreal this morning will reach Chatham junction early to-morrow morning and will connect with the train for Fredericton. That means that the residents of the county of Northumberland can go to Fredericton, spend four or five hours in the city and come back the same night. Those who live near the western border of the county complain that they have not the necessary railway connection between Newcastle and Chatham on the east, and Boiestown and Blackville on the west. If a merchant living at Boiestown or Doaktown wishes to go to Chatham to do business he cannot get into Chatham and back the same day but he must go down on the train which arrives in Chatham about five o'clock, or on the express which arrives at about eleven o'clock. If he wishes to do any business, he has to remain all night in Chatham, all

the next day and all the next night and go up the following morning because there are no trains going west after bank hours. The people of the county have requested, they have petitioned, they have prayed, that the Government give them a train starting at Boiestown, or, better still, at Fredericton, to leave Boiestown in the morning and return in the evening. The Government, with good reason, I suppose, have not acceded, saying that there is not sufficient business for it. The trains do run the other way, for- the reason that they must be run to make connection with the express and mails for and from Fredericton via Chatham Junction. But, if the Government were disposed to be liberal, surely one additional train could be put on. There is a surplus, and surely this railway is not to be run as if it were a private concern and make everything pay that we do. Now, engineer Matheson was on train No. 99, and he knew very well 'that Smith could not be very far, because he was kept at Sayabee so as to give Smith sufficient time to get away, and his duty was to slacken speed so as to prevent an .accident. Between Sayabee and St. Moise there is an ascent of five miles, followed by a descent of three miles, when coming to St. Moise. As Smith's train was coming into St. Moise at a speed of ten miles an hour, he saw coming towards him in the rear, at great speed, train No. 99. As his orders were to meet train No. 76 at St. Moise, and in order to avoid an accident with the train which should be in front of the station, he was forced to slacken the speed of his own train to ten miles an hour, thereby acting in the way of prudence and acting'according to the rules. He has been censured for not having properly protected his train, but he could not do that, because there is no necessity to protect a train under way, especially when running at ten "miles an hour.

I can not offer an opinion on the management of the Intercolonial. I think I have said enough to express my opinion on Mr. Brady's management. The hon. Minister of Railways told us that the employees of that railway had associations to protect themselves. I know that such associations are in existence, but it is very well known what a costly experiment it is to bring them into action. The president of the Brotherhood lives in the United States and it takes month after month before you can reach him; and during that time the unfortunate heads of large families are kept out of work waiting for the association to deal with the question. Moreover, it is very important to have as managers of the railway, men who can settle such questions without waiting for the interference of the association.
For the last thirty-five years we have had a man who was general manager of the Intercolonial. I am referring to Mr. Pottinger. His management met with the approval of both French and English Canadians. I, myself, have had occasion to meet him frequently and I have always found him a perfect gentleman, very agreeable in his dealings with all.
He would receive us in his office like gentlemen, and although we did not always get satisfaction, although we sometimes failed to get what we asked for, we left him happy and contented, because we had the answer of a fair and clever man. I am sorry to see such a man leaving the service of the Intercolonial while such a man as Mr. Brady is being kept on. Mr. Pottinger is still in full possession of his mental and physical strength. He knows the Intercolonial from the first mile to the last; he is friendly with everybody in the maritime provinces as well as in the province of Quebec. I have known him since 1875, and I am sorry to see him retired. I hope he asked to be retired, but I cannot believe it

unless I am told so by himself. We will never have a more devoted servant of the country than he was.
It is said that since Mr. Brady has been appointed Chairman of the Board there is no more deficit. That is true, but it must be borne in mind that Mr. Pottinger was there when the road was created. The fact is that he built and equipped the road. There was a surplus then, but everything was to be done. He must have had to submit to political influences and must have had to do things that he would not have done had he been left to himself. With Mr. Brady it is quite the reverse. When he was given the management of the road he was also given leave to do as he liked. He has cut heads off; he has cut down everywhere and he has increased the freight rates. ^Moreover, the traffic has increased largely." It was there the same as elsewhere. Twenty years ago the revenue of the country hardly reached 35 millions; to-day it is 160 millions. Everything has increased in proportion and the revenue of the Intercolonial like the rest. And still we are told that the surplus is due to Mr. Brady's management. It seems to me that is not fair.
During my long experience on the Intercolonial I have not known of one single employee who has ever criticized the decisions of Mr. Pottinger, even when he was not satisfied. I must give him that credit publicly. He deserves it.
As to Mr. Caron, whose dismissal is deplored, I would certainly prefer to see him remain at his post, to having nobody put in his place. Mr. Brady should make room for a French Canadian.

Everybody has been out of order all afternoon. What we have been discussing chiefly is the operation of the Intercolonial railway instead of the capital account. With reference to the new arrangement, the situation is that Mr. Gutelius is not a commissioner, as I understand it, he is general manager. The old arrangement is reverted to, namely, that of having one general manager, the only difference being that Air. Gutelius is that officer instead of Mr. Pottinger. An error is often made in calling the board, which has been in operation for some years, a commission. A commission was in the platform announced by the right hon. the Prime Minister. He was to have a board of commissioners to manage the Intercolonial. I think that was in his Halifax platform. Some fault was found with the administration of the late Government because the board was not made a commission. The difference between a managing board and a commission in brief is that a commission would be responsible to Parliament while a board is responsible to the minister. I prefer the board idea to the commission idea, because I do not believe that even by engaging a general manager the minister can get away from responsibility for whatever is done on the Intercolonial Tailway. The idea of that board is based on what Is done by several of the leading railway companies. They have a board that meets .regularly. It is made up of the heads of the different departments, and these plan the policy, and carry it out. On my recommendation, the late Government tried that experiment in connection with the management of the Intercolonial railway. It had its weaknesses, but I maintain that a vast improvement was made in the administration of the Intercolonial under the board on which each department had its head. In the working out of the scheme a weakness was found, which was that we had no man on the board to handle the legal end of the business. Hon. members of this House who were then members will recollect that a Bill was introduced giving to the local courts in the various provinces

through which the Intercolonial runs power to try suits against the Intercolonial up to a stated amount. That was an advanced step. Before the Act was passed, no matter how small the claim a man residing along the Intercolonial might have against the railway, it was a claim against the Government, and the Government could only be sued in the Exchequer Court, and then only if a fiat had been issued. So the modus operandi of a man bringing suit against the Government railways was expensive and tedious, and as a result there was a great deal of complaint amon'gst those who had sustained losses. An Act was passed placing the trial of these small cases within the jurisdiction of the local courts. That necessitated a legal man on this board. I looked about for a man who was not only a man of good legal attainments, but I thought it was essential that he ought to be able to speak both languages, and Mr. Caron filled the bill in both respects. I admit that, having served in Parliament for a number of years, I have a tendency to giving the preference to one who has been an associate in parliament, because the great majority of members of parliament, notwithstanding anything that is said to the contrary, make sacrifices for the country and, everything being equal, it is not unjust that they should be given the preference in a matter of this kind. Mr. Caron was given the position with the approval, I think, of every member of the House at the time, because I cannot recollect one objection being taken to his appointment. I think that the press on both sides endorsed his selection.
In dismissing Mr. Caron and appointing a mah in the city of Montreal the minister does not meet the difficulty with which he is confronted. The difficulty is that the Intercolonial railway cannot have, with the consent of the Justice Department, a man in the city of Moncton to handle all the legal cases. Some adjustment ought to be made by which one legal gentleman would be able to handle the legal business of the Government railways without all these cases coming to the city of Ottawa for adjustment. From the practical railway standpoint there should be a legal head at the head office of the Government railways, just as there is a legal head at the head office of the private railways. Until this is done there will not be satisfaction in the settlement of claims against the Intercolonial railway. The Justice Department ought to work out a scheme by which all Intercolonial legal business shall be handled by the legal head at the headquarters of the railway. This business should not go through the Justice Department except in some particular cases. That Mr. GRAHAM.
being so, the appointment of one man to look after this business is a necessity, and I do not know of any man better fitted for the position than Mr. Caron. The appointment of a man in the city of Montreal will only mean that he will attend to the cases around the city, and the cases fifty miles away from Montreal will be sent to local legal men by the Department of Justice. If there are half a dozen cases coming on in any one district how is a man in Montreal going to attend to them all? He will send these cases to a man in the locality in which they arise and that, no doubt, is a better way to do it. But tne only way to have them settled properly i* in have a man at the head office of the Government railways! with full pow'ar to handle the legal business of these railways and let him select, just a3 the Justice Department does now, if a case is to be tried in Montreal or at some point where he cannot attend, or is not expected to attend, a representative to look after it. That is the only possibly solution of the question.
If my hon. friend undertakes to handle the legal business of the Intercolonial railway through the Department of Justice there will not be satisfaction. As it is the Justice Department is overburdened with work. We have had a new department added to it recently, and a portion of the money might better have been devoted to the establishment of a legal department for the Government railways. If the minister will work out the scheme along that line he will find a satisfactory solution. One reason why the Government is troubled with all these claims is that there is no man in Moncton who has power to settle them. Even Mr. Caron had not power to settle them. But he did a lot of good work along the line of settling claims without allowing them to come to trial. The legal department might be more usefully employed in settling than in defending suits. There should be some centre of legal authority on the line of the railway so that the public would not have to appeal to the Department of Justice and go through all the red tape in order to secure the settlement of the case. If you had a legal department you could perhaps reach a settlement in twenty-four hours in the case of a man who might otherwise become a litigant, and the only way to accomplish this is to have a legal department established at Moncton. The Department of Justice is not in favour of this because it is contended, and perhaps with some reason, that the Department of Justice is responsible, that it represents the Growrw that this being a Government railway, it is the Crown's, and that, consequently, the legal

business cannot go through any person else. I will admit that the Justice Department is in a measure responsible, but it might have a man at Moncton with power to settle all these claims. I believe that the legal department, the railway department and perhaps the Prime Minister could get together and work out a scheme by which the legal business of the Intercolonial railway could be handed over to a man competent to take charge of it at Moncton, and who would be empowered to settle all claims that came in. I submit that Mr. Caron would be a good man to put in that position because he has had a great deal of experience in that particular line oi work. I think that if the minister takes this up with the Justice Department he will find that the proper solution of the problem is to work out a scheme with their consent u'hereby a legal department will be established at the head office at Moncton with full powers to act and to settle all claims.

I do not wish to prolong this discussion more than is necessary, but I feel that the Minister of Railways would not wish to do an injustice to Mr. Caron. I suppose the hon. member for L'Islet will say in private what he has just stated in the House publicly this afternoon: that he would raise no objection to the reappointment of Mr. Caron in the capacity of legal adviser to the board at Moncton. Not many years ago another gentleman who had been a very prominent man in the province of Quebec against the liberal government, was defeated; he had been a member of the House for nearly a quarter of a century; he appealed, and not in vain, to the Government of the day. We found for him a good position as counsel, not in the Civil Service,
I admit, but through the influence of the Government, in a large corporation. I say this only to confirm what the ex-Minister of Railways has stated, that old members of Parliament who have received Government appointments should be protected and not he made the victims of party exigencies. In |

The effect of the procedure is to exasperate the officials of the department who seem to think the whole idea is to prevent the farmers from getting his claim, and, what, is worse, it is exasperating to the claimant who thinks he has a good claim against the road. It may be said, perhaps, that they do not pay anything they can get out of paying, but the point is that you can get a settlement with them. I have done so in hundreds of cases; sometimes I go to the claims agent or perhaps to the head office in Montreal. The matter is threshed out as a matter of business, and we settle it almost always. But it is practically impossible to do anything with the Intercolonial railway. There is so much red tape that by the time you do get a settlement, the people concerned have almost forgotten what they were talking about. There seems to be a disposition on the part of the officials-I do not know why-to act as though the organization were there to prevent the settlement of these cases. You will never Mr. CARVELL.
succeed in obtaining a settlement of these claims on a reasonable basis until you have a claims agent or a claims solicitor-if the minister would rather leave it in the hands of a solicitor-but whether a claims agent or a claims solicitor, he ought to be a man in whom some power is vested. Heretofore, all the man could do who went down to investigate was to report. Sometimes he gets the facts, and sometimes he does not. I wish to say a few words upon this item. On the occasion, nearly two months ago, when Parliament was asked to vote one-sixth of this amount, I addressed myself briefly to the committee upon the same matter. At that time-I said to the hon. minister and to the Government that I strongly protested against the manner in which the announcement of this proposed expenditure for terminals was made at Halifax, in October last. As I remarked on that occasion, possibly the minister himself was not altogether to blame. It was, however, made the occasion of more or less political jubilation on the part of his friends in that city. This project involved a very considerable expenditure and was an important undertaking, and the announcement, I submit, should have been first made to Parliament, or, failing that, to the public interested, in a frank, comprehensive and businesslike manner, which I claim was not done. The announcement was premature, and clearly for political effect. Concurrently with
344J
the ministerial announcement to which <1 refer, appeared a statement made by the Halifax Herald, a paper friendly to the Administration, that the total expenditure contemplated for the Halifax terminals would amount to $35,000,000. This estimated expenditure was never contradicted or qualified by anybody speaking on behalf of the Department of Railways. The citizens of Halifax consequently, considered that this amount would be expended for steamship and railway terminals at Halifax. This statement of the amount to be expended by a newspaper believed to be speaking for the Government naturally had an effect upon the public. Naturally the proposal to expend such a large sum of money for terminals was gratifying to the people of Halifax and it apparently had the effect of suppressing for a time, any general criticism of the details of the project, although considerable unexpressed doubt existed in the minds of many as to such details. I fear that many persons honestly concluded, that any criticism of the scheme would be construed into opposition, and they preferred for a time, silence to misconstruction. Opposition to the mode of affording the port of Halifax the terminals required, gradually developed, until now I am advised and believe it is quite substantial. This, I venture to say, might have been largely obviated, or would.have culminated more quickly, which would perhaps have been to the advantage of the Department of Railways had the minister taken the public more largely into his confidence, and have afforded them the reasons for the adoption of the terminal scheme as announced. I do not know whether or not there should be any favours in this country, so far as real favouritism is concerned, but I do contend that the Dominion Steel Corporation having been given in its earlier days a schedule of freight rates over the Intercolonial railway that were somewhat lower than the ordinary rates, that at this particular period of the history of that institution the freight rates should not be raised. The Dominion Steel Corporation, like other new corporations in this country, has much to contend with. The gentlemen who saw fit to put their money in the new scheme of manufacturing steel on the harbour of Sydney were given certain privileges by the people of the city of Sydney and by the Dominion Government in the shape of tariffs and of bonuses, they were also granted certain privileges by the Government of Nova Scotia, all those things were done at that time with a desire to influence the men interested in the Dominion Steel Corporation to start operations in this country. in the sheds at Sydney has been raised one hundred per cent, and now the corporation has as much as it can do to make both ends meet. It was granted those privileges with the idea of influencing these men to put their capital into the enterprise. These institutions are up against a proposition that not only are they not receiving those bounties, but also they are finding that they are compelled to pay higher rates of freight. I contend that every dollar that the Dominion Steel Corporation are obliged to pay over to the railway over and above their freight rates of the past, is a dollar taken out of the workmen of eastern Nova Scotia, because if the Dominion Steel Corporation has to pay more freight they will certainly have to make a decrease in their wages in order to make both ends meet. I think it is most unfair that this institution, the Dominion Steel Corporation, having been given the idea that they were to have a cheap rate over the Intercolonial railway, should at this particular period of its history be made to pay a higher rate than they have hitherto paid. The eastern section of the Intercolonial railway is the best paying part of that railway, or if it is not the best it ranks second only to the Montreal-end. I say it is discouraging to capitalists who have placed their money in this province, it will discourage future capitalists from doing so under the idea that they are getting certain privileges and, as representing the constituency where the Dominion Steel Corporation carries on its business, 1 protest to the minister and this Government, I protested when this news gained currency, that it is unfair not only to this corporation but to eastern Nova Scotia and unfair to the workingmen of Nova Scotia. The steel corporation of Sydney has been instrumental, [together with the coal company, in building up good towns in Sydney, Glace Bay and other parts of the country. These towns afford markets for the farmers of Nova Scotia, not only of Nova Scotia but of Prince Edward Island and the eastern section of New Brunswick and I think it is rather discouraging that the Minister- of Railways should see fit to make this change in view of the fact that this end of the line is one of the very best paying sections of the whole road. I can only add my word of protest against this increase so far as the eastern section of Nova Scotia is concerned. What does this mean? It means this, further, that the Intercolonial railway are not going to gain- anything by this change, for I dare say the Dominion Steel Company will hereafter ship as much as they can by water rather than submit to this increase in freight rates over the Intercolonial railway. If the Intercolonial railway were going to gain by this increase it would not be so bad but I believe the

railway will be the loser. The corporation are bound not to pay such a high tariff and having that in view they will endeavour in every possible way to make all shipments from Sydney by water.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Bonaven-ture has just complained of the want of freight cars on the Intercolonial. For my part I have received a great many complaints about this. In days gone by it was sought to make the Intercolonial pay by cutting down the expense for the purchase of cars and even of engines. That was the way they tried to get a surplus. I am glad to find a substantial increase in the amount to be voted this year for rolling stock. I have even strong doubt of the amount being sufficient. Traffic has increased and is constantly increasing on the Intercolonial, as elsewhere, for that matter, and moreover there are new branches built Which are using our cars. In that way t'he Baie des, Chaleurs, Intercolonial and Caraquet railways are using our cars to carry their freight. Instead of supplying cars for the service of those lines connecting with the Intercolonial, it would be more practical and more in the interest of the country to buy these branch lines of railway. We are already supplying them with the cars they need. The Intercolonial could operate these railways cheaper than they can be operated by the companies; it already has the necessary plant, such as shops, &e., and it could realize better profits than the companies. Flavie to Matane, the International, the Caraquet railway, the Baie des Chaleurs railway, I mean the road that goes from Metapedia to Gaspe. I hope that means will be taken to purchase these branches and thus increase the profits of the Intercolonial.

I defy the hon. member for Queens to stand up and say he is not in favour of the position I am taking, that the minister should take over the operation of the- winter boats, cut down the freights and give advantage in regard to transportation of goods which he says he proposed to do when the car-ferry is in operation.

I asked if the contracts
for the ship and for the piers have (been let?
Will these amounts complete the piers and the boat ready for service?
That is the understanding.
I suppose when my hon. friend speaks of widening the gauge of the Prince Edward Island railway the proposition is to introduce a third rail until the present rolling stock has been worn out?

I had an engineer all summer working on the question of the car-ferry but I have not had an examination as to the third rail or the conversion of the Prince Edward railway to standard gauge. You would practically have to rebuild the road to put on the third rail.
Hudson Bay railway-construction and terminals,-$4,500,000.
How much of this is for railway construction and how much for terminals?

The contracts as let,
as near as we can get at them, are: from the Pas to Thicket Portage,	500,000, one
hundred and eighty-five miles; from Thicket Portage to Split Lake Junction, $1,000,000; from Split Lake Junction to Hudson bay, $1,000,000. That is as near as we can get at the cost of rne railway at present, that is from the Pas to Nelson.

This vote is enough for
the whole construction then?

We have got to put
in something for the harbour work. We expect to send a number of men with supplies and a complete plant down this year

to start the development of the harbour there, they nave dredges and cement and a regular plant for the development of the harbour.
