$1,500,000. We do not expect to spend all of it this year.

And how much is it
estimated that the harbour improvement will cost?

I have not a definite estimate. The trouble is to get into communication there. I propose to put a wireless station at the Pas and one at Nelson. The one at the Pas we can move to some other place afterwards when we get the land lines through. The one at Nelson we will, of course, require permanently. We have only had one communication since navigation closed last fall, since I came out in fact, and I cannot say definitely what the total cost will be.
It is definitely decided to establish the terminus at Port Nelson?

Yes, it is so much
shorter than the other route. There are seventy miles of barren land on which it is difficult to say how the operation of a Tailway would act. It is frozen, and I think there are from three to seven or eight feet of muskeg on the top. It would be difficult to get over.

I think the Government
is not well advised on deciding on Port Nelson until information is at hand as to what the cost will be of establishing proper harbour facilities at that point. My information is that the expense will be stupendous, and that under no circumstances can an entirely satisfactory port be established at Nelson.
That is not our report.

The reason being that there are many miles of shallow water from the shore until deep water is reached. There will have to be a dredged channel tor
some ten or fifteen miles, to enable vessels to enter the harbour at the mouth of the river. It is absolutely impossible that vessels can reach the sheltered mouth of the river by way of that dredged channel in any hut calm weather. That, as it appears to me, is a tremendous objection to the establishment of Port Nelson, as the terminus of the railroad. At any rate, I want to place before the Government my view that they should have the fullest information as to what the cost will be before they begin to make large expenditures. There is no doubt that at Churchill there is a harbour at the present time, a harbour easy of access, and safe when reached, not large, but possibly large enough for any reasonable requirements. I quite appreciate what the minister says against Port Churchill. The distance is greater, and there are certain questions as to railroad construction. That, of course, must be admitted, but on the other hand we know that there is a practicable harbour at Churchill; we know that 'if we are to have a practicable harbour at Nelson it will have to be made, and I say again that we ought to know what it will cost to make that harbour before we make large expenditures upon it. I understand from the minister that he proposes to spend a million or a million and a half of dollars upon that harbour, and as much of that amount as possible during the current summer without having full information as to what the expenditure required to complete the work will be. If that is the position, I think it is hardly a desirable position.

The hon. gentleman
has got some wrong information. Shortly before I arrived at Nelson last year, the Minto was up within a mile, I think of the place where it is proposed to have the harbour. There is a channel there, over twenty feet deep, and there is no aid to navigation. There are no buoys or anything of that kind to guide a vessel up to the harbour. That matter will have to be straightened to some extent, and buoys will have to be put in to guide a ship up. I do not intend to go on with any elaborate expenditure until we know something definite about the navigation. If we are sure on that point, wre will go in and make a permanent place, but until we find out about the navigation and see what benefit it is going to lie as our grain route, I would not care to go to any great expense there. But I saw the place myself. The water is shallow, but the channel is there, and it can be made more navigable without a great deal of dredging. They propose to run a pier out into the stream rather than dredge, because they think it would be cheaper to do so.

The hon. minister has
made a remark which appeals to my mind very strongly. He says he does not propose to make any very great expenditure in connection with the harbour at Port Nelson until he has assured himself that that will be a satisfactory harbour. That will certainly be an act of wisdom, and I trust he will retain that idea in connection with the building of the so-called Hudson Bay railway, and will not proceed with any lavish expenditure in connection with that railway until he has absolutely assured himself that its construction will work to the advantage of Canada generally. I am one of those who doubt that the construction of the Hud-

son Bay railway will be of one dollar's worth advantage to Canada.
Hear, hear.

The wheat from the Northwest cannot reach the British market by the Hudson Bay railway and Hudson bay during the year in which it is grown and harvested. It could only get through Hudson bay in the following year. I maintain that if you satisfactorily deepen the St. Lawrence navigation route you will get a transportation route, which, together with the railway facilities that we have, will carry to Great Britain every bushel of grain likely to be grown in the Northwest during the next 100 years, at a cost less than you could carry it over the Hudson bay route, and it would be carried at a much more rapid rate, so that it would reach Liverpool earlier than grain carried by any Hudson bay road you can build. Although this Hudson bay route was suggested by the late Government, I was opposed to it, and I am opposed to it to-day, and until I see some evidence more clearly showing that the construction of that railroad will be to the general advantage of Canada, I shall retain the opinion I have always had, that it will not be to the general advantage of Canada. The history of that country teaches us that the Hudson bay is not navigable except for about three months in the year.
It never freezes.

But the straits are impassable. No boats carrying wheat from the Northwest would ever attempt to go through there, excepting for about three months of a year. No insurance company would insure them. It is to my mind an absolutely impracticable route, and I am not alone in saying that. I have asked men of wide experience and wide knowledge, of much wider knowledge and experience than I have. Such a scheme, as a financial proposition and as a scheme for the general advantage of Canada, is absolutely absurd and it is throwing money into a hole. It is an absolute waste of material. Let us use our money to better advantage. I trust that my hon. friend, pursuing the policy which he has announced with reference to Port Nelson, will use some degree of wise discretion in regard to the construction of the railway and not spend very much money or go ahead rapidly until he has absolutely satisfied himself, as the level-headed business man he is, that the construction of the railway would be for the general advantage of the country and that the money cannot be used to much greater advantage in the building up of our water transportation.
Mr. GERMAN.

Having had the pleasure of travelling over that section of northern Canada last year, I feel that I should not allow this opportunity to go by without saying a word with regard to it. While perhaps the opinion of a man of my years would, not weigh as much as that of the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver), or of the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Cochrane), or of other older gentlemen, I may say that I have formed a conclusion in regard to this subject that is the result of personal observation and study. In this connection let me point out that the report issued by the Senate in 1905 or 1907, gave a very large amount of information in regard to that north country, to which information I gave particular study last year. I am of the opinion that the Hudson Bay route is navigable for four or four and a half months in the year, and that any expenditure which this or any succeeding Government may make with regard to the extension of a railway into that section of Canada in order to make that route available, will in the future result in immense good to the country. Fort Churchill, as the hon. member for Edmonton has stated, is one hundred and fifty miles north of Port Nelson and is only five hundred miles in a direct line irom the heart of the Peace river valley, an area seven hundred miles long by one hundred and fifty miles wide, and possessing, according to statements by agriculturists of the most advanced knowledge, probably the finest agricultural land in Alberta. Let us consider that Fort Churchill is some fifty-eight miles nearer to Liverpool by water than is New York, let us consider that the heart of the great provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan is within a five hundred rail-haul of water communication, that the products of that great country can be placed in a ship at Fort Churchill and Port Nelson and transferred across the water by a route which is admittedly fifty-eight miles shorter than from New York to Liverpool, and we must come to the conclusion that these conditions are bound to contribute to the greater development of Canada in the future. Few hon. gentlemen apparently have given the matter sufficient study to warrant them in coming to a final opinion in regard to the matter. In consulting the records in regard to the natural resources of that section of the country, we get an idea of its tremendous area and the variety and volume of its products. The United States consul at Kingston or Toronto, I forget -which, in Dreparing data for the United States Government in regard to the forest belt of nortnern Canada, describes what he calls the spruce belt of Canada, as running from Labrador north-westerly to

Alaska, a stretch of land in area some fifty-four times larger than the state of New York and possessing untold millions of feet of timber, spruce, fir, pine and birch. That is not all. In that great northwestern country there are 3,000 miles of inland navigable waterways which can be connected by the building of a short line of railway of only thirty miles and that inland water communication, at present navigable, is only five hundred miles from Fort Churchill and some seven hundred and fifty miles from Port Nelson. When we consider the fact that the isothermal lines in northwestern Canada do not run east and west, as I venture to suggest hon. gentlemen have believed offhand, but run north and south and that, therefore, the ability to raise wheat and vegetables has been demonstrated as far north as within fourteen miles of the arctic circle in the great Mackenzie valley, we can picture with some degree of accuracy, we can prophesy with some degree of certainty, what the future of this great section of the Dominion will be. The question which presents itself to my mind is whether or not the expenditure of a million or two millions in the Hudson Bay district will not be the percursor of expenditures which will contribute to the building up of a larger Canada in that great northwestern section of this continent than we have at present under civilization. From what study I have given to this subject I am profoundly enthusiastic over the great possibilities of this northern country. I am profoundly impressed with the belief that any expenditure wisely made by this Government or by succeeding governments cannot but contribute to the future development of the country.	[DOT]
One word more and it is in regard to the point that was made by the hon. member for Welland (Mr. German) on the question of the navigation of the Hudson'Bay route. He says that he does not think that the-straits are navigable. It has been demonstrated that the Government steamer went in there in the early part of July and that it came out on the 5th of November last year. We know from personal observation that we have found greater obstacles in the straits of Belle Isle and north of Belle Isle, where steamers operate in the early part of the summer, than we found going through the Hudson straits on our trip last year, and from which I gained a most favourable opinion as to the feasibility of that route. Some information has been given us by Captain Bartlett who went through the straits on the Minto. It must not be forgotten that instead of a day of ten or twelve hours they have in that north country a day of nineteen hours or twenty hours and at some seasons of the year they have not more than three hours of night. All these things taken together must convince anybody who
studies the question that this expenditure in that country is a worthy undertaking and that it will redound to the benefit of the Dominion generally.

I think it would cost almost as much to do what I propose doing at Nelson as it would at Churchill. I was at both places and it is shallow out a long piece and there is no channel at Churchill. I think it would cost at much at Churchill as it would at Nelson, and of course it would take a great deal to build the railway eighty-five miles further.

It would certainly cost
more to build the railway to Churchill. I am not quarreling with the minister because he is making an attempt at Nelson. I appreciate the advantages of Nelson if it is practicable, but I want to guard against the supposition that Nelson is the only alternative.
I understand that.

I am pointing out that
there are certain difficulties at Nelson and I would be glad to see them overcome. If they are not satisfactorily overcome and if they cannot be, then there is no doubt that a practical port can be found at Churchill. One point in connection with Churchill is that it is more directly accessible to the Peace river country than is Nelson. When the Peace River country is developed, Churchill would be the natural port for that country, and it would give the Peace river wheat region closer access to the ocean, that than Manitoba has to-day, and thus cheapen the cost of the transportation of the product of that country.

It is a very barren
place?

No doubt, but still the
isothenpal lines in the western part of the central country run [DOT] far north, so that directly west of Churchill is a wheat-growing country when you reach the Peace river. How many miles of the railway are actually under grading at present?

The bridge across the Saskatchewan river was unfortunately only

finished last month and they only commenced this month to lay the track. 1 have not a report as to the number of miles of track laid. I think the grading is done for 100 and some odd miles; we hope to have the rails on the first 185 miles this fall.
Will the work be opened up beyond that point this summer?
They have provisions in to work on any rock work there may be found there.
How many men are employed?
Speaking from memory the last report said there were between 400 and 500 men.
Are there any heavy bridges on that 185 miles?

There are quite a
number of bridges, but I do not think any large ones. -

Lest my silence might
be construed that I have lost faith in this work, I may say that I have still faith it will be a practicable and profitable undertaking and if I had not I would not have committed the country to the expenditure. I would go so far as to say that the railway should be constructed even if it had not any steamship connection to Europe. Railways have been constructed in different parts of Canada where' there is far less prospect of doing business than in connection with this project. Irom what I know of the country and the prospect of traffic from the bay I would be in favour of building the line even if there were no ocean ports there at all. I always favoured Nelson from the informa>
tion I had in the department, and that view seems to be confirmed. If the traffic is to assume any dimensions at all-and unless the department were satisfied it will, they would not go to the expense of having very costly terminal facilities there-if the traffic is to assume any proportions a good harbour is necessary, and from the information in the department the best harbour is to be found at Nelson, provided the difficulty referred to is overcome. I -would not say that navigation would be opened for four and a half months, but it has always been my opinion that it will be open for between three and a half and four months, and even at that it will relieve the congestion very materially.
And I would like to point out to the doubting Thomases this:	they refer to grain
only; but the dairymen and stock raisers cf eastern Canada may well keep in nrn 1 the fact that that part of the West is goinsr to be a great dairying and stork raising ccun-Mr. COCHRANE.
try. Nobody need tell me that stock that can be put on shipboard with a rail haul of two cool nights and one day and then taken by a cool route to Liverpool, will not be in better condition than if carried by a long rail haul. The amount saved in shrinkage would alone be a large item. All this must be taken into consideration when we are thinking about the effects of this route.
And there is the import.

Yes, there must be the return cargoes to the West. Even if we say that it is only for three, or three and a half, or four months in the year, I cannot see but that the expenditure will be in. the interest of the people of Canada not only of the West but of the East as well. Is the minister any nearer to arrangements for a steamship connection than he was a year ago?
That is hardly in my line. I have been urging it on the Government, but I do not know that much has been done. We shall have to subsidize a line-
No doubt.

And we shall have to-give what some people regard as a heavy subsidy; but to have a proper test, this will have to be done. This is going to help out Nova Scotia and the East, especially in the shipping of steel rails to the West. There is a steamer haul of two thousand miles from Sydney to Nelson, and then a rail haul of six or seven miles would distribute over quite a large country in the West.
Where are the rails purchased for this road?

At Sault Ste. Marie, Of course on a shipment by way of Fort William, we get a much lower freight rate than the other way. Until we get a wharf and a track and have other facilities for handling freight, the rates by the other way would bte very high, because handling freight by lightering it out in small boats is very expensive. I think I am safe in saying that it takes $3 to do what $1 would do with proper facilities.
Are the wireless stations to be built this summer?
The one at Port Nelson goes up 6n the first boat, and the one for Le Pas is ordered now. By means of these we can keep in touch and get information.

I wish to say a wordin favour of the Hudson Bay railway, as I was a member of the Government which first encouraged this national undertaking. When the Canadian Pacific railway was

started thirty years ago there were many doubting Thomases, and yet events have proven that it was a successful national undertaking. When the Grand Trunk Pacific was started under the leadership of the present leader of the Opposition there were many who predicted that it would be a huge failure, yet to-day we are not satisfied with two transcontinental lines but are building a third, and probably shall be asked within a day or so to help that third line. When the people of the West are clamouring for the construction of the Hudson bay railway, and when, according to the experts, there is a legitimate expectation that it will bring relief to that section of the country which is building up so rapidly, and which in twenty-five or thirty years will be the home of millions of people from all parts of the world, I think it is only fair that the Government should begin now to provide for the future. What I wanted to lay emphasis upon was this further fact that, when you have completed the Hudson Bay railway from the centre of the prairie region to the great sea of Hudson, when you have reached Port Nelson you will be face to face with this difficulty that the straits will be kept open only for a limited period of the year.
I do not think that has been definitely settled.

It has not been dealt with definitely, and I do not suppose it will be in the near future. It is admitted, however, that the straits cannot be kept open for a long period of time. Once the grain has reached the shores of Hudson bay, if the straits are closed up, I believe the next 'best thing to do is to build a railway from the head of James bay to Montreal, tapping the Transcontinental at Cochrane.
No, it would be farther east of Cochrane.

East of Cochrane, and from there to Montreal or Quebec, then working in conjunction with the existing main lines in this section of the country. The Hudson bay itself-I am not speaking of the straits-is navigable for at least eight months in the year, according to the reports. Grain can be shipped more cheaply by water than^by rail. You can certainly save a large amount of money on big shipments of grain via the Hudson bay from Port Nelson to the head of James bay. If you have a railway from James bay to Montreal or Quebec, which will put this whole railway system in communication with the eastern parts of Canada you have found the key, the solution to the transportation problem of Canada during summer and winter. I hope the hon. minister will look favourably upon that project.
The legislature of the province of Quebec has heavily subsidized that section of our transportation system between James bay and Montreal. It will develop the resources of northern Quebec and I think, at least incidentally, part of northern Ontario. That region, which I had the advantage of visiting last summer, strikes me as being very rich and capable of a vast development. The government of the province of Quebec has opened up new townships in that region, and already a large number of settlers have gone there. The reports received so far are most favourable. This railway system from James bay to Montreal, working in conjunction with the Hudson bay railway is bound to be a great success in the near future. That is why I vote, without any hesitation, the necessary moneys for the construction of the Hudson Bay railway. I care not whether it benefits the West; I sincerely believe it will benefit the country as a whole. What benefits the West, benefits the East. For my part, as a member of the late Government, I claim some credit for having with my colleagues shaped the policy in favour of the construction of the Hudson Bay railway. If the present Government will continue in our footsteps, I will say * Yea ' with great pleasure.	[DOT]

Will the hon. minister give me some information with respect to the expropriation of land at St. Peter's canal? The minister was good enough to place the file in my hands. I cannot understand, however, why the award made by O'Dwyer, who was sent down by the department to value those lands, was revised by three men in'Lhe town of St. Peter's, all of whom are personal and political friends of Mr. J. A. Gillies, the defeated Conservative candidate, who owned the land. The hon. minister stated to me last year that, if the owner of the land was not content with the valuation placed on it by that gentleman, the matter would have to go to the Exchequer Court.

I sent Mr. O'Dwyer
down there as he had done good work as valuator for the Intercolonial. When his report came in, I thought it was high, just as the hon. gentleman stated in the House, and so I apointed the others. Their award was very little less than Mr. O'Dwyer's. I was aware, when the second award came in, that we would have been in a difficult position had we gone to the Exchequer Court at that time, because they could have summoned these men and produced their valuation. I have in the supplementary estimates a sum for a valuator of the department, whom we can send around. He has been working on the Intercolonial and has done good service. He will soon have completed his work there.

Will the hon. minister tell
me who recommended those valuators at St. Peter's?
I cannot give the information at present, I could look it up in the department.
I presume these appointments would come through the person having the patronage in the county of Richmond?
Absolutely no.
The recommendation would rather suggest that.
No.
How long will it be before the road will be completed to the bay?
They have taken the contract to complete it next year. From the progress they have made I question whether it will be finished then or not.
Is there a reasonable prospect of its being completed by 1915?
Yes, I do not think there is any doubt about that.

Is there any mention of
reaching Split Lake in advance of railway construction?

I think there is a way up. They go up Lake Winnipeg; there is a chain of lakes which they use in order to strike the railway very near there. I think Split Lake will probably be the next point to which they will move their headquarters in the fall.
Have the locations of the terminals at the Falls been decided upon?
Yes, on the south side.
Are they acquired from the Indian reserve?
Yes, the Indians are being given valuation on their property. I hope it will not be too high. I do not think their land is worth much.

The question has been
raised here in regard to the cost of this railroad, the charge upon the treasury. Some years ago the principle of pre-emptions was introduced into the western country, with the understanding that the fund accruing from the sale of pre-emptions would be considered as an extra source of revenue from which the Hudson Bay railway might be constructed. There was no ear-marking of money received. When the policy of sale of pre-emption was introduced, it was introduced with the understanding that a new source of revenue was being created which would relieve the general treasury from the cost of the Hudson Bay railway. Therefore the treasury of Canada is not Mr. COCHRANE.
finding* the money for building the railway. It is the land of the Northwest and the price that is being paid for that * land that is building the Hudson Bay railway; and enough money is being taken out of preemptions in the West to pay for that railway. I think it is just as well to have that statement made.
The road will be built anyway.

I want to relieve the assertion that the road constitutes a serious charge upon the finances of the country. As a matter of fact, it does not. Another point was that the grain that was raised in a certain year cannot go forward by the Hudson bay route during the same calendar year. That is measurably true, but it is also true with regard to grain going forward by the St. Lawrence route. Only a portion of the year's crop goes forward during the calendar year in which it is grown. I think it is safe to say that by far the larger part goes forward after having lain in storage not less than four, five, six or seven months. Therefore the disadvantage of the Hudson bay route in that particular is not serious. The disadvantage of navigation of Hudson straits is spoken of. Surely Hudson straits are more easily navigable during their proper season of navigation than the straits of Belle Isle. The straits of Belle Isle are three or four miles across while the Hudson straits are from forty miles to one hundred miles across. Yet an enormous traffic goes through the straits of Belle Isle when they are open. It is dangerous but it is short and much traffic is handled that way. In the Hudson straits there are disadvantages but they cannot be as great as in Belle Isle and the shortness in distance compensates for the disadvantages. The Hudson bay route was for two hundred years the only route by which could be reached what is now our prairie west and if it was adequate for the purposes of that trade during that time with the means of navigation that then existed, surely it will be of advantage under present conditions where the needs are so very great and the means of navigation have so greatly improved. In any case, it is a matter that may be talked about interminably without any conclusion being reached. The only way in which the question will ever bje solved will be by laying the rails from the wheat fields to the bay, and the sooner the rails are laid to the bay the better for the country and the greater the credit to this Government.

I think the greatest difficulty that navigators will experience will be drift ice and fog. I do not think the straits ever freeze over, from all the information I can get, but the raft ice and

fog during a portion of the year are very bad. You cannot do much even with wireless where you have ice. If it was only fog, if the straits were free of ice, you could have wireless stations and guide the steamers tip through the straits but where you have both it will be very difficult.
We will go on with these estimates to-morrow?
I think we will take up ithe militia estimates and the Justice Department estimates to-morrow. An understanding to that effect has been reached between the whips.
Could the Justice Department estimates be taken up, as I want to be present when the militia estimates are taken up, and I have to attend the Railway committee for some time in the morning.
Yes.

We have been accustomed to having an interim report of the Transcontinental commission, giving the work up to date on the construction of the line. On the item for the Welland canal, I presume the Minister of Public Works will be able to announce the policy of the Government in connection with the Georgian Bay canal.
